paras.text: These adhesives form a bond by the application of light pressure to adhere the adhesive with the adherent. Once the adhesive and the adherent are in close proximity, molecular interactions, such as Van der Waals forces; become involved in the bond, contributing significantly to its ultimate strength. Major raw material for pressure sensitive adhesives (PSA’s) are acrylate-based polymers. It is mainly used in safety labels for power equipment and automotive interior trim assembly.

paras.text: These are also known as hot melt adhesives (HMA) or thermoplastics and are applied in molten form (65 – 180°C range) which solidify on cooling to form strong bonds between a wide range of materials. Hot adhesives containing ‘ethylene vinyl acetate’, are particularly popular for crafts because of their ease of use and the wide range of common materials they can join. A glue-gun is one method of applying hot adhesives. Hot-melt adhesives are commonly used in bookbinding, for the manufacture of packaging, for coatings, diapers, other sanitary products and tapes.

Synthetic adhesives are not found in nature and are designed and manufactured by man. Typical synthetic adhesives are epoxies, polyurethanes, cyanoacrylates, polyimides, silicones, acrylics, polyacrylates, polyvinyl acetate (PVA) and neoprene.

2. Natural Adhesives (Glues)

Natural adhesives are those adhesives that are obtained or extracted from natural resources such as plants or animals, starch, casein glues or natural rubber etc.

Classification of Adhesives on Reactiveness

Adhesives are mainly classified into two classes on reactiveness.

1. Non-Reactive Adhesives   2. Reactive Adhesives

The basis of classification is their method of adhesion.

1. Non-Reactive Adhesives

These adhesives may be either of natural or synthetic origin. Drying adhesive, pressure sensitive adhesives, contact adhesives and hot adhesives are some examples of this class.

i. Drying Adhesives

There are two types of adhesives which become hard by drying.

a. Solvent Based Adhesives: Which are a mixture of ingredients (typically polymers) dissolved in a solvent. White glue, contact adhesives and rubber cements are the members of the drying adhesive family. It is used for binding of the woods and papers.

b. Polymer Dispersion Adhesives: These are also known as emulsion adhesives and are milky white dispersions often based on polyvinyl acetate (PVAc). These are extensively used in the woodworking and packaging industries. They are also used with fabrics and fabric-based components and in engineered products such as loudspeaker cones.

ii. Pressure Sensitive Adhesive (PSA)

These adhesives form a bond by the application of light pressure to adhere the adhesive with the adherent. Once the adhesive and the adherent are in close proximity, molecular interactions, such as Van der Waals forces; become involved in the bond, contributing significantly to its ultimate strength. Major raw material for pressure sensitive adhesives (PSA’s) are acrylate-based polymers. It is mainly used in safety labels for power equipment and automotive interior trim assembly.

iii. Contact Adhesive

These are used in strong bonds with high ‘shear-resistance’ like laminates, such as bonding formica to a wooden counter and in footwear, as in attaching outsoles to uppers. Examples of contact adhesives are natural rubber and polychloroprene (Neoprene).

iv. Hot Adhesives

These are also known as hot melt adhesives (HMA) or thermoplastics and are applied in molten form (65 – 180°C range) which solidify on cooling to form strong bonds between a wide range of materials. Hot adhesives containing ‘ethylene vinyl acetate’, are particularly popular for crafts because of their ease of use and the wide range of common materials they can join. A glue-gun is one method of applying hot adhesives. Hot-melt adhesives are commonly used in bookbinding, for the manufacture of packaging, for coatings, diapers, other sanitary products and tapes.

Importance of Adhesives

A number of miscellaneous tasks in our world require gluing together of things. They reduce the cost. Industrial adhesives are extremely strong and they can be used in place of more complicated repair works. Adhesives are efficient. They do not tamper with the integrity of the substance. In fact, they only make it stronger. They can be applied to any kind of material. Adhesive are divided into the following types.

Figure 22.2 Types of adhesives.

Classification of Adhesives by Origin

Adhesives are divided according to their origin, therefore, we have synthetic adhesives and natural adhesives.

1. Synthetic Adhesives

Synthetic adhesives are not found in nature and are designed and manufactured by man. Typical synthetic adhesives are epoxies, polyurethanes, cyanoacrylates, polyimides, silicones, acrylics, polyacrylates, polyvinyl acetate (PVA) and neoprene.

2. Natural Adhesives (Glues)

Natural adhesives are those adhesives that are obtained or extracted from natural resources such as plants or animals, starch, casein glues or natural rubber etc.

Classification of Adhesives on Reactiveness

Adhesives are mainly classified into two classes on reactiveness.

1. Non-Reactive Adhesives 2. Reactive Adhesives

The basis of classification is their method of adhesion.

1. Non-Reactive Adhesives

These adhesives may be either of natural or synthetic origin. Drying adhesive, pressure sensitive adhesives, contact adhesives and hot adhesives are some examples of this class.

i. Drying Adhesives

There are two types of adhesives which become hard by drying.

a. Solvent Based Adhesives: Which are a mixture of ingredients (typically polymers) dissolved in a solvent. White glue, contact adhesives and rubber cements are the members of the drying adhesive family. It is used for binding of the woods and papers.

b. Polymer Dispersion Adhesives: These are also known as emulsion adhesives and are milky white dispersions often based on polyvinyl acetate (PVAc). These are extensively used in the woodworking and packaging industries. They are also used with fabrics and fabric-based components and in engineered products such as loudspeaker cones.

ii. Pressure Sensitive Adhesive (PSA)

These adhesives form a bond by the application of light pressure to adhere the adhesive with the adherent. Once the adhesive and the adherent are in close proximity, molecular interactions, such as Van der Waals forces; become involved in the bond, contributing significantly to its ultimate strength. Major raw material for pressure sensitive adhesives (PSA’s) are acrylate-based polymers. It is mainly used in safety labels for power equipment and automotive interior trim assembly.

iii. Contact Adhesive

These are used in strong bonds with high ‘shear-resistance’ like laminates, such as bonding formica to a wooden counter and in footwear, as in attaching outsoles to uppers. Examples of contact adhesives are natural rubber and polychloroprene (Neoprene).

iv. Hot Adhesives

These are also known as hot melt adhesives (HMA) or thermoplastics and are applied in molten form (65 – 180°C range) which solidify on cooling to form strong bonds between a wide range of materials. Hot adhesives containing ‘ethylene vinyl acetate’, are particularly popular for crafts because of their ease of use and the wide range of common materials they can join. A glue-gun is one method of applying hot adhesives. Hot-melt adhesives are commonly used in bookbinding, for the manufacture of packaging, for coatings, diapers, other sanitary products and tapes.

These adhesives harden by mixing two or more components, which chemically react. Commercially, there are several combinations of multi-component adhesives that are

a. Polyester resin-polyurethane resin
b. Polyols-polyurethane resins

One Part Adhesives
These adhesives harden through a chemical reaction with an external energy source such as radiation, heat or moisture. Light curing adhesives are generally acylic based and due to their rapid action, they are significantly used in electronics, telecommunications, medical, aerospace, glass and in optics.
Heat curing adhesives include epoxies, urethanes and polyimides, while moisture curing adhesives cure when they react with moisture present on the substrate surface or in the air. These types of adhesives include cyanoacrylates and urethanes.

Industrial chemistry is the study of fundamental chemical processes used in industry for transferring raw material to useful commercial products for society. Dye is a substance, which adds value to product for their cost.
Pesticides are chemical substances used for destroying insect and other organisms harmful to cultivated plants or to animals.
Petrochemicals are chemicals derived from petroleum products and used in the

A polymer is a macromolecule formed as a result of a process known as
polymerization.

Cosmetics are chemicals, which are intended to be applied to the human body for cleansing, beautifying or altering the appearance without affecting the body's functions.
Lipstick is mainly composed of a mixture of non-volatile oil and solid wax. Nail varnish or nail polish is a lacquer applied to human finger nails or toe nails to decorate or protect the nail plate.

remover.
